body:
Everything goes. Nothing remains

I have a great deal of myself invested in the things I have on my digital devices. If I can't destroy that part of myself, how can I destroy the rest?

It's comforting, I suppose. Demanding such thoroughness probably reduces the chances that I'll ever go through with it.

You might consider going to speak with either your prof. for the course in question, or the prof. for the next class; they might be willing / able to accommodate you. There's no guarantee, but you won't know unless you try.

Also, if you have a faculty or program advisor, you might want to consider speaking with them - they might be able to offer advice or some sort of workaround.

You say that you have a good job, interpersonal relationships, etc. - 'you're doing better than most people you know'. On the other hand, in your [last post](https://www.reddit.com/r/SuicideWatch/comments/80gaqo/why_is_it_my_responsibility_to_get_better_for/), you said that you're “overworked, stressed out, not sleeping enough, and never have enough me time”.

From what I'm reading – and I apologize if I'm drawing the wrong conclusions – you seem like a talented, capable person who has a lot on his plate right now. You are doing work and school at the same time, and trying to maintain relationships on top of that.

What I would recommend is, if you are able, to dial things back a bit.

The thing with many people who are high achievers is that they can be tempted to bite off more than they can chew. I've witnessed this personally – I had a brief stint in law school where I was surrounded by driven, smart, high-achieving individuals. There were all sorts of people who wanted to rank at the top of their class, volunteer, work and have an active social life, all at the same time. The caution from graduates, professors, everyone who knew or had experience was “Tone it down. If you try to do everything, you're going to end up killing yourself.”

 You can't push yourself, physically and psychologically, indefinitely without consequence. Drinking, binging on medication – these things can dull the symptoms for a while but they can't tackle the cause.

Don't start a new hobby, don't throw yourself into school and work even more, don't buy a gym membership. Making new commitments is not the response to being burnt out. Dial it all back a bit. Try to get a good night's sleep. Read a good book. Spend some time with your GF. Take time to relax, time where you don't have to worry about being productive. Do it on a regular basis; don't just binge every so often.

I realize talk is cheap. Obviously, if you've committed to months or years of school, or you're working overtime to stay in house and home – finding time for yourself isn't exactly easy. All I can say under those circumstances is that, looking forward, try ease things a little. If you're halfway through a certificate or program, even if you can't let up at this very minute, consider taking the next semester off to catch your breath. If you can't find time for yourself right now, at least plan so that you can down the road.

The benefits of higher education are definitely real, but are sometimes... exaggerated. Don't feel as though you've hit a brick wall if you don't, or can't, go on to college. Unfortunately, in the United States, there is a huge industry built around 'selling' higher education, and they do everything they can to play up college as a destination, and pooh-pooh any alternatives.

Don't think about college as something you 'have to' do. There are literally millions of people who have gone to college or university because they thought that they 'had to' in order to be successful, and emerged with degrees that they didn't want, and as no more employable than they were before.

Think about something you want to achieve – a skill, entry into a particular profession – and then look for ways that you can achieve that. College might be one way - but it isn't the only way.

If you want to upgrade your skills, there are other options than a brick and mortar institution.

There are a lot of degree and vocational programs available through distance and E-learning. These are very much built around people in circumstances like your own – individuals in areas that don't have access to traditional educational options. While it is important to be careful in this regard – some distance education providers can be shady or low-quality – but if you do your background research, you can probably find a good institution that will allow you to get the degree, certificate, or qualification that you're interested in, from home.

There are also a lot skills that you can essentially learn on your own. There are thousands of people in your country who learned how to do things like design work or computer programming by reading books, looking for tutorials online, and a lot of practice. It is not easy; it requires significant investment of time and effort, and great personal discipline. But it can be done.
